records.text: A fork, and a clean one. One piece attacks several targets at once, and the defense must deal with all of them.
A costly lapse. It hands the other side a fork, one of their pieces attacking several targets at once. Find the square where that piece lands.
A fork was there to be taken, one piece striking several targets at once. This move leaves it on the table. Go back and find the square.
That is a proper pin. The piece in front of its king cannot step off the line, because doing so would expose the king behind it.
A real concession. The other side can now pin a piece to its king, and once pinned, the piece is held to that line.
Another move pinned a piece to its king. Pinned like that, it could not leave the line without exposing the king. This move lets the chance go.
A skewer, well aimed. The front piece is attacked, and when it moves, the piece behind it is exposed.
This leaves two pieces on one line for the other side to skewer. When the front piece moves, the one behind it could be exposed.
A stronger move had a skewer. Attack the front piece, and when it steps aside, the piece behind it is exposed. This move does not use it.
This is the right target. Capture the defender, and whatever it protected loses that protection.
The other side can now capture a defender. When it falls, whatever it guarded could lose its protection. Know which pieces depend on it.
The defender was the target, and another move could have captured it. Whatever it guarded would have lost its protection. This move leaves it standing.
A back-rank mate idea, and a sharp one. The king is hemmed in by its own pieces, with no square to run to.
The back rank is weak, and this move lets the other side use it. The king's own pieces block its escape, and that is a route to mate.
A back-rank mate was available, with the king boxed in by its own pieces. This move passes it up. A finish like that should not be missed.
The pawn has a road to the last rank, and the aim is to promote it. Follow that road square by square.
This gives the other side a path to promotion. One of their pawns can now head for the last rank. Stop pawns like that early.
A stronger move cleared the way for a pawn to reach the last rank and promote. This move ignores that road.
A discovered attack, and a forceful one. One piece steps out of the line, and the piece behind it attacks. Two threats from one move.
One of their pieces is screening another, and this move lets the screen lift. Stepping aside uncovers an attack from the piece behind.
Another move had a discovered attack: shift the front piece, and the one behind it strikes. This move keeps that threat hidden.
Two attacks with one move. That is forcing play, and the defense has to answer both at once.
This allows a double attack. The other side can make two threats with one move, and a single reply has to meet both.
A stronger move had two attacks ready at once. This move lets that double attack go to waste.
Deflection, executed well. The defender is pulled away from its post, and what it was covering is left open.
A defender carries a vital task, and the other side can now drag it away. That is a deflection, and the task would go uncovered.
A stronger move could have dragged a defender away from its post. That deflection was the better idea, and this move does not use it.
A piece stood without a guard, and the move takes it. A loose piece is an invitation; this move accepts it.
An undefended piece was there to take with another move. Nothing guarded it. Loose pieces must be checked before every move.
This leaves a piece without a guard, and the other side can take it. Every piece must be accounted for before a move is made.
This move pulls away a piece's only real defender. The other side can now capture what was left unguarded. Know a defender's duty before you move it.
The threat came with the opponent's last move, and this move does not answer it. Now a piece is there to be captured. Read the opponent's move before you make your own.
This trade loses value. The capture invites a recapture of a more valuable piece. An exchange is judged at its end, not its first move.
A minor piece comes off its starting square and joins the game. A piece left at home does no work.
Another move would have brought a minor piece out from its starting square and into play.
The rook takes an open file, with no pawn of either color on it. That is where a rook belongs.
Another move would have put a rook on an open file, clear of pawns of both colors.
The rook stands on a semi-open file. None of its own pawns block it, and at least one enemy pawn remains there to press against.
Another move would have set a rook on a semi-open file, free of its own pawns, with an enemy pawn still on it.
This creates a passed pawn. No enemy pawn stands ahead of it on its own file or either neighboring file. Passed pawns must be pushed or stopped.
Another move would have created a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or the files beside it.
The passed pawn marches on. It was already free; now it is closer to the last rank and harder to ignore.
Another move would have pushed the passed pawn forward, closer to the last rank.
The move leaves a pawn isolated. No friendly pawn stands on either file beside it, so only pieces can defend it.
Another move would have left an isolated pawn, with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file.
A piece that stood without a defender now has one. Keep your pieces protected.
Another move would have given an undefended piece the protection it lacked.
A piece is now without any defender. That alone does not mean it can be won, but it is now a target to watch.
Another move would have stripped a piece of its last defender. Even so, that alone would not prove the piece could be won.
The king gains a legal flight square it did not have before. An escape square is worth having.
Another move would have opened a new legal flight square for the king.
The king castles, and the rook comes across with it. Both pieces move in a single turn.
Castling was the alternative, moving king and rook in a single move.
The capture ends the bishop pair. That side no longer has a bishop for each color of square.
Another move would have taken a bishop and broken the other side's bishop pair.
This leaves doubled pawns, two pawns of one color on the same file. They cannot protect each other.
Another move would have doubled a side's pawns, stacking two of one color on the same file.
This move is fatal. The other side now has a forced checkmate. Trace the attack back to the moment the defense gave way.
A forced checkmate was on the board, and this move lets it go. When the king is trapped, finish the job. Go back and find the mate.
A sacrifice with real substance. In the line that was checked, taking the offered material does not refute it. That takes nerve and calculation.
Exact defense. Of every move checked, only this one kept the position playable; the others were losing. I respect that.
This move alone held on to the advantage. The other moves checked were losing. Precision like that is what wins games.
The reply captures at once. Something is left to be taken, and it should have been seen before moving.
The strongest reply comes with check. The king must be answered first, and that check belongs in every calculation.
This is not the best. The engine prefers another move, and its replies tell a different story. Set the two side by side.
This move falls short of the engine's best. The reply shows where the value leaks away. Find it.
Strong, and properly so. Among the moves the engine examined, this one gives up almost nothing. That is the standard to hold.
Sound, though not the best. The engine prefers another move, but this one keeps most of what the position offered.
A natural move, by the human-move model, and still the wrong one. The engine has a stronger move here. Natural choices need the same scrutiny as any other.
The human-move model rarely expects this move, and the engine rates it strong. Unusual and sound. That has my approval.
One move kept the position playable, and it was missed. The human-move model grades that defense hard to find. Hard defenses are still defenses; study this one.
A hard move to find, by the human-move model and the alternatives checked. Remember it, so the next one comes easier.
This move held the position. The human-move model and the searched alternatives both mark it as a hard defense to find. Well defended.
Natural, according to the human-move model, and the engine's best move as well. Here the natural move is also the correct one.
A natural move by the human-move model, and a strong one by the engine, though another move ranks higher.
Very little time was left on the clock before this move. Pressure like that tests everything.
A quick move, with time still in hand. Speed is only worth it when the move is right.
A long think went into this move. Time is a resource; spend it where the position demands it.
This move belongs to a recognized opening line. Known ground, but knowing the name is not the same as knowing the position.
The game leaves the opening book here. From this move on, judgment has to replace memory.
After the earlier setback, this move brings the position back to playable. That is fighting back, and it counts.
After the earlier setback, the position is back to playable. The other side's errors helped. Take the gift, but do not rely on it.
The opponent's last move left an opening, and this move takes it. Errors are there to be punished.
The opponent's last move offered an opportunity, and this move lets it pass. When the other side errs, make them pay.
This same issue has already appeared in this game. An issue that keeps returning is a habit forming. Compare the moments and find the warning sign.
The piece that was left unguarded earlier has support again. Keep it that way.
No single blunder did this. Several small concessions have worn the position down, and this is one more. Small losses add up.
The advantage held through every reviewed move, all the way to the win. Converting cleanly is a skill, and this was done well.
This issue appears in other saved games as well. It is a pattern now, and patterns must be broken. Study those games beside this one.
Checkmate, with no legal escape for the king. The attack is complete.
Checkmate, and the king has no legal square left. The defense failed earlier; go back and find where it could have held.
A draw. The result is settled, but the decisions that led here still deserve a hard look.
Study the position. When you are sure, commit to your move.
That attempt does not hold up. Look again, and calculate more carefully.
That attempt returned no result. Go back to the move and try it once more.
The saved engine analysis finds a forced checkmate for the side that made this move.
The saved engine analysis gives the other side a forced checkmate once this move is made.
By the end of the saved line, the side that made this move has won material compared with where it started.
By the end of the saved line, the side that made this move has lost material compared with where it started.
This exercise accepts the move. The moves shown give no clear tactical reason, so do not invent one.
This move is not accepted for this exercise. The moves shown give no clear tactical reason, and I will not pretend they do.
The move matches one of this exercise's saved answers. Here, the saved answers set the standard.
This move is not among the saved answers for this exercise. That does not make a different legal move bad chess; it only falls outside what this exercise accepts.
Study this move until you understand it. Then take on the next position.
A good move, then. Know why it works, not just that it does.
Your practice is saved, and the review schedule stays as it was.
Solved, but this recall still stays marked for relearning. One success is not mastery.
This is where it begins, before any of the moves under examination. Take the position in fully.
Here is the next move. Look at what it changes on the board.
A check. The king is attacked, and everything else waits until that is answered.
With this move, the king steps out of check.
The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes to a new piece.
The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes, and the move gives check as well.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and it is checkmate. The king has nowhere left to go.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the same move takes its own king out of check.
A capture: this move takes a piece.
This move captures a piece and gives check in the same stroke.
This move captures a piece and delivers checkmate. The king has no escape.
This move captures a piece, and the capture takes the king out of check.
The pawn captures on its way to the last rank and promotes.
The pawn captures, promotes on the last rank, and gives check, all in one move.
The pawn captures and promotes on the last rank, and that is checkmate. No legal escape remains.
The pawn captures and promotes on the last rank, and the same move frees its king from check.
The king castles, the rook comes across, and the same move delivers check.
The king castles, the rook comes across, and it is checkmate. The other king has no legal escape.
This is a fork that pays. One piece attacks several targets, then takes one, and this example ends with a net material gain.
The piece is pinned to its king, so it cannot make the capture that is marked. Leaving the pin line would expose the king.
The attacked piece is pinned against its king. Its escape is limited to moves that keep the king covered, and that narrows the defense.
The capture works because the defenders are pinned to their king and cannot take back. In the line shown, material is gained.
The pinned piece cannot leave its line without exposing its king. It is held there, and as these moves play out, it is captured.
The front piece moves off the line, and the piece behind it is captured along that same line. That is the skewer doing its work.
Check drives the king off the line. The same attacker then takes the piece that stood behind it.
First the only defender is captured. Then, later in these moves, the piece it guarded falls too. Remove the guard, then take the prize.
The defender is drawn away from its task, and the piece it was guarding is then captured.
The blocking piece moves, and a capture comes along the line it opened, made by the piece behind.
One piece steps out of the line, and the piece behind it gives check.
A double check. Two pieces attack the king at once, and only a king move can answer both.
The moved piece makes one attack and opens a line for another. In this example, the second piece captures its target.
The pawn promotes, and in this example that side finishes with a net material gain.
The piece had no defender, and it is captured. In this example, the capturing side ends with a net material gain.
The opponent's previous move freed the attacking piece from a relative pin. The target stayed where it was, and in the line shown it is captured.
The other side has the marked reply available, and it is legal. Play it, and see what it does to the position.
Before every move, find any piece of yours that could be captured without a useful recapture.
Before settling on a quiet move, check for enemy pieces left without a guard.
Search the forcing moves for one piece that attacks two valuable targets at once.
Before moving a pinned piece, know what stands behind it: the king, or something more valuable.
An attack does not stop at the first target. Look along the line for a valuable piece standing behind it.
Before trading off a defender, know exactly what it protects right now.
A blocking piece that moves opens lines behind it. Know where every one of them leads.
Search for one move that makes two threats at once. Checks and newly opened lines count.
Before a back-rank defender moves, check that the king still has an escape square.
Count the moves a pawn needs to promote, and calculate every forcing pawn advance.
Before a defender moves, list everything it protects. Each of those pieces loses that protection when it goes.
Count the full exchange: what the capture takes, and what the recapture takes back.
Check whether a forcing exchange can drag a defender away from another target it guards.
This exercise is judged by its saved answers. A different legal move can still be good chess; it simply is not what this exercise asks for.
The moves shown are played against strong replies. Strong is not the same as forced, so do not treat every reply here as the only one.
The material changes apply only to the line shown, measured from its starting position. The piece values used are listed in the written explanation.
No simple tactical reason comes out of the saved line. Step through it and compare the replies yourself; no positional explanation has been assumed.
The answer policy saved for this exercise governs this explanation. Its setting is in the written notes.
Here are the moves of the opening line you are studying. Learn them well enough to play them without help.
Right. That move belongs to your selected study material.
The answer lies in the study lines you selected. Play a move from them.
More than one move from your selected opening lines is accepted here. Play any one of them.
Your selected study material holds the move for this position. Bring it back from memory.
That move is not in the opening lines you selected to study. Make another attempt.
That move lies outside your selected opening lines. Make another attempt. This saved attempt does not update the changed study's review schedule.
That move lies outside the opening lines you selected. Attempt it again. This position is retired, so its review schedule stays unchanged.
In mixed Due, this line's moves are accepted. Dedicated practice demands this line alone.
Scheduled recalls will ask for the moves of your selected side. Where active studies share a position, they share a single card.
Reload the saved session first. Only then make your next move.
The verified line is playing on the board. Watch every move of it.
The solution was revealed, and the attempt is saved that way. Replay the solution below, and learn it properly.
Solved on a retry. The earlier miss and the finish both stay in your record. Next time, find it first.
The full solution, with no wrong move. That is how a puzzle should be solved.
Not the solution. Your correct moves before it stay saved.
Right so far. The puzzle is not finished; find the next move.
Calculate before you move. A puzzle rewards precision, not haste.
The engine has not given me enough to explain this position, and I will not guess.
Your review is on pause. Resume it below, or move a piece and explore the position.
Select a move to review it, or move a piece to test an alternative.
This move stands in established opening theory.
Theory knows this move. It belongs to a recognized opening.
This is a recognized opening move. Theory can name it, but it cannot play the position for you.
Theory still holds here.
Another established move.
The reply is established theory as well.
The known lines carry on.
Still within established theory.
The established line runs on.
Theory has not run out yet.
One more move theory already knows. Knowing a line and understanding it are not the same.
The human-move model finds this move natural, and it is fatal. The other side now has a forced checkmate. Trace the attack back and find where the defense gave way.
A forced checkmate was on the board. This move is the natural one by the human-move model, and it lets the mate go. When the king is trapped, look for the finish before anything else.
The human-move model expects this move, and the reply captures at once. An obvious move still has to survive the obvious reply.
Natural, by the human-move model, and still weaker than the engine's best. Part of the position's value is gone. A move that looks right must still be checked.
The human-move model finds this move natural, and it hands the other side a fork, one piece attacking several targets at once. The fork does not care how natural the move felt.
A natural move, by the human-move model, and it leaves two pieces on one line for a skewer. When the front piece moves, the one behind it could be exposed. Check your lines before you commit.
Exact defense. Every other move checked was losing; this one kept the position playable. The human-move model grades it a hard defense, and it was found anyway. That is defending at a high standard.
The only move that kept the position playable. The others checked were losing, and the human-move model and the alternatives both mark this one as hard to find. Found, and found correctly.
Only this move kept the advantage; the other moves checked were losing. The human-move model rates it a hard resource to find. A difficult move, played when it mattered.
No other move checked kept the advantage, and every one of them was losing. The human-move model and the alternatives rate this a hard find. Precision under pressure. I respect it.
A fork, one piece attacking several targets at once. The human-move model rarely expects the move, and the engine rates it strong. Unusual, and fully justified.
A fork, and the engine's best move. One piece hits several targets at once. The human-move model and the alternatives mark it as hard to find, which makes finding it worth more.
A pin against the king. The pinned piece cannot leave its line without exposing the king. The human-move model seldom predicts this move; the engine calls it strong. A bold choice that holds.
The engine's best move, built on a pin to the king. The pinned piece is stuck on its line. By the human-move model, a hard move to find. Good work.

The human-move model calls this move natural, and it pulls away a piece's only real defender. The other side can capture what was left behind. Know a defender's duty before you move it, however natural the move looks.

This move takes away a piece's only real defender, and the other side can capture it. A single searched move would have kept the position playable. The human-move model rates that defense hard to find. Hard or not, it is the one to learn.
The threat was set by the opponent's last move. This move is natural by the human-move model, and it ignores that threat, so a piece is now open to capture. Answer the opponent's move first.

The opponent's last move created a threat, and this move leaves it unanswered. A piece is now there for the taking. Only one move checked held the position, and the human-move model marks it as difficult. Study that defense.
The capture is natural, by the human-move model, but the recapture takes a more valuable piece. A trade is only good when the whole of it is good. Count both halves.

The capture here invites a recapture of something more valuable. A different move was the only one checked that kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Compare it with the full exchange.
A fork, one piece attacking several targets. The human-move model calls it natural, and no move beats it in the engine's search. The obvious move and the right move are the same here.
A fork, with one piece reaching several targets. The human-move model finds it natural; the engine finds it strong, though another move ranks higher. Good, but not the best.

This hands the other side a fork, one of their pieces attacking several targets. Only one searched move kept the position playable, and it was missed. The human-move model rates it a hard find. That defense deserves study.

Another move had a fork, one piece striking several targets at once. This move is the more natural one to the human-move model, and the fork goes unplayed. Search for forcing moves before natural ones.

The only searched move that kept the position playable carried a fork, one piece attacking several targets. That move was passed over. The human-move model marks it hard to find. Go back and find that piece.
A pin to the king, and the engine's best move. The pinned piece cannot leave the line. To the human-move model, it is the natural choice. Natural and best together is what you want.
A pin to the king: the pinned piece must hold its line. The human-move model expects the move, and the engine rates it strong, with another move first. Solid, though not the top choice.
The other side can now pin a piece to its king, and once pinned it cannot leave the line. To the human-move model this is a natural move. It still gives away too much.
This hands the other side a pin against the king. Of the moves checked, only one kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Find that move, and learn why it holds.
A stronger move would have pinned a piece to its king, freezing it on its line. This move is the natural choice by the human-move model, and the pin goes unused. Look for the stronger idea first.

A pin to the king was the heart of the one searched move that kept the position playable. It was missed, and the human-move model rates it a hard find. Hard defenses are still defenses. Learn this one.
A skewer, and the engine's best move. When the front piece moves, the one behind it is exposed. The human-move model and the alternatives mark it hard to find. Well calculated.
A skewer: attack the front piece, and the one behind it is exposed when it moves. The human-move model rarely predicts this move, but the engine rates it strong. It stands on its merit.
Two pieces on one line, and a skewer through both. The human-move model's natural choice, and the engine's top move. Exactly right.
A skewer along the line. The human-move model expects the move; the engine rates it strong, though it prefers another. Strong, not best.

The other side can now skewer two pieces on one line; move the front one, and the one behind could be exposed. Only one move checked held the position, and the human-move model grades it a hard find. That is the move to study.
Another move had a skewer: move the front piece, and the one behind it is exposed. This move is natural by the human-move model, and the skewer is left on the board. Look along the lines first.
The only move checked that held the position contained a skewer, and this move passed it by. By the human-move model, it was difficult to find. Return to it until you can see it.
The defender is captured, and what it protected stands exposed. The engine ranks this move best, and the human-move model and the alternatives call it a hard find. That is a sharp eye.
The target is the defender. Capture it, and its protection is gone. The human-move model does not expect this move; the engine rates it strong. Unusual, and correct.
Capture the defender, and what it guarded loses its protection. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine puts nothing above it. No hesitation needed here.
A defender is captured, and its protection ends with it. The human-move model favors the move, and the engine grades it strong, with one move above it.
A defender can now be captured, and whatever it guards could lose its protection. To the human-move model this move is natural. That does not make it safe.

The other side can now capture a defender. One move among those checked kept the position playable, and it was not the one played. The human-move model grades it a hard find. Find it anyway, and remember it.
Another move could have captured a defender and stripped away its protection. The human-move model expects this move instead, and the defender keeps its post. Go after the defenders.
The only move checked that held the position captured a defender. It went unplayed, and the human-move model rates it hard to see. That defense is worth your time.
A back-rank mating idea, with the king hemmed in by its own pieces. This is the engine's best move, and the human-move model and the alternatives mark it hard to find. A finish worth respecting.
The king's own pieces block its escape, and this move uses the back rank. The human-move model does not expect it; the engine calls it strong. A bold move with a sound reason.
A back-rank mating idea, the king walled in by its own pieces. Natural by the human-move model, and nothing in the engine's search beats it. Clean and correct.
The king is trapped behind its own pieces, and this move aims at the back rank. A natural move by the human-move model, and strong by the engine, though not its first choice.
A pawn has a road to the last rank, and promotion is the goal. This is the engine's best move, and the human-move model grades it hard to find. Pawns like that win games.
The pawn is on its way to the last rank, aiming to promote. The human-move model rarely expects this move, and the engine rates it strong. Unexpected, and right.
Promotion is the aim, with a pawn driving toward the last rank. The human-move model calls the move natural, and the engine's search ranks nothing higher. Push it with purpose.
A pawn's road to the last rank is the point. The human-move model rates the move natural. The engine rates it strong, with a different move ranked higher.
This move is natural by the human-move model, and it gives one of their pawns a path to the last rank. The other side can now try to promote. Stop a pawn like that early, not late.
This opens a road to promotion for the other side. Of the moves checked, only one kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. That defense is the lesson here.
Another move opened a pawn's road to the last rank. This one is more natural by the human-move model, and the promotion chance is left unused. Count the pawn's moves before anything else.
The one searched move that kept the position playable would have pushed a pawn toward promotion. This move passed it by. The human-move model marks it as hard to find. Learn to see that road.
A discovered attack, and a sharp one. The blocker steps aside, and the piece behind it strikes. This is the engine's best move, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Strong work.
A blocker moves, and the attack behind it is unleashed. The human-move model would seldom choose this move, yet the engine grades it strong. Unusual, and sound.
A discovered attack: the front piece moves, and the one behind it attacks. The human-move model's natural choice, and the engine's best. Exactly the move.
A blocker steps off the line, and a discovered attack opens. The human-move model calls it natural. The engine grades it strong, though another move ranks above it.

One of their pieces is screening another, and this move lets it step aside with a threat from behind. The human-move model treats it as the natural move. Natural or not, the discovered attack is there.
This allows a discovered attack for the other side. Only one move checked kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it hard to see. Make that defense part of your study.

A stronger move would have uncovered an attack, with one piece stepping aside for the piece behind it. The human-move model favors the move played, and that attack stays buried. Check every line a piece could open.

The only move checked that held the position uncovered an attack, one piece stepping aside for another. This move went elsewhere. The human-move model rates it difficult to find. Work through it until it is clear.
Two threats from one move. A double attack, and the engine's best. The human-move model and the searched alternatives say it was hard to find. That is forcing chess.
One move, two threats at the same time. The human-move model would rarely pick it, and the engine grades it strong. Bold, and sound.
One move, two threats, and the defense has to deal with both. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine has it as best. Simple and strong.
A double attack, two threats in one move. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine calls it strong, though another move ranks first.
Two threats can now come at once, a double attack for the other side. The human-move model calls this a natural move. A single reply has to answer both threats.
This allows a double attack, two threats arriving together. One defense held among the moves checked, and it was missed; the human-move model rates it hard to find. Study it.
A stronger move had two threats in it at once. This one is more natural by the human-move model, and the double attack goes unplayed. Two threats beat one quiet move.
The only move checked that kept the position playable made two attacks at once. It was missed, and the human-move model rates it hard to see. Go back and find both threats.
Deflection. The defender is drawn away, and what it covered is left open. The engine's best move, and the human-move model and the alternatives call it a hard find. That earns real respect.
A defender is pulled away from what it protects. The human-move model seldom predicts the move, and the engine grades it strong. Unusual and correct.
Draw the defender away, and its task is abandoned. The human-move model finds the deflection natural, and it is the engine's first choice. Well played.
The defender is lured away from what it guards. The human-move model calls the move natural. The engine rates it strong, but prefers another.
A defender can now be dragged away from its task, a deflection for the other side. To the human-move model, it is the natural choice. What that defender covers could be left open.
The other side can now pull a defender from what it guards. Only one move checked held the position, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. That is the move to learn.
A stronger move could have dragged a defender off its post. The human-move model favors the move played, and the defender keeps its post. Know what each defender is guarding.

The single move checked that kept the position playable was a deflection, pulling a defender away. This move went another way, and the human-move model grades the deflection a hard find. Return to it.
An undefended piece, and the move takes it. The engine ranks it best, and the human-move model marks it hard to find. Seen and taken.
There was an undefended piece to take, and this move takes it. The human-move model rarely expects the move; the engine calls it strong. A loose piece, collected.
